_comment: The cookbook page's bottom matter (2026-08-24): one entry per recipe — where it came from and one line of the house's voice. Display content only: no rule reads this. Parsed by RecipeLore (LastCall.Game) with loud validation; RecipeLoreTests pins ids to RecipeCatalog both ways.

entries.note: Lean the glass, let the keg talk, straighten for the head. The head is the craft.
One bottle, no tin, no argument. The order for people who already know the answer.
The lightest thing a bar can legally call a drink. Clean, cold, gone.
Spirit, lemon, sugar — the oldest equation behind half this book.
Quinine against malaria, gin against quinine. Empire's most useful accident.
Bourbon with a cola chaser that gave up and got in the glass.
Named for the tool that stirred it first. Breakfast in some ports.
Vodka over coffee liqueur, invented for an ambassador with dark hours to keep.
Vodka and energy in one glass — a drink working the day shift and the night shift at once.
Rum, cola and a lime for a free Cuba. The lime is not a garnish; it is the point.
Bourbon lengthened with ginger — the highball that made whiskey a weeknight drink.
A vodka salesman and a ginger-beer surplus invented Russia's most American drink.
Gin and lime cordial, first dosed against scurvy, later against boredom.

entries.origin: MADRAS, BY WAY OF NEW ENGLAND, 1960S
entries.note: Vodka under cranberry and orange. Named for a cloth, not a city, and nobody minds.
The gin sour with the lights turned low. Smoother crowd, same lemon.
Grenadine sinks, orange floats, and the Rolling Stones took it on tour.
The sour that made bourbon polite. The backbone is not optional.
Rum, lime, sugar, shaken cold. Hemingway kept a tab open on it.
A gin sour with soda's doors open. Ramos shook his for twelve minutes.
Vodka, triple sec, lime, no survivors. Served up, because it is a cocktail and not a shot.
Tequila, orange and lime behind a salted rim. Nobody agrees who; everyone agrees why.
The pink one. Cranberry keeps the vodka honest and the glass photogenic.
The Ritz claims it, London disputes it. Ours runs on whiskey and does not apologise.
One of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak. Older than the glass it sits in.
Gin, triple sec, lemon — Harry MacElhone's silver-shaker standard.
Gin, lime and mint. The outfit drank it; the mint hid the bathtub.
Gin barely troubled by vermouth, stirred cold, finished with a twist. The measure all bars are taken by.
A martini that came with supper. The spear is the whole difference, so do not forget it.
Whiskey and sweet vermouth, stirred. The cocktail wearing the city's name tag.
Count Negroni asked for a harder Americano. Equal parts, no negotiation.
Sugar, bitters, whiskey — the drink the word 'cocktail' was coined for.
'Wake me up, then mess me up.' Dick Bradsell obliged with a shaker and the coffee bottle.
Trader Vic poured it neat over crushed ice; the islands added the fruit. Ours keeps the fruit.
Mint bruised, lime squeezed, rum rewarded. Drake's crew allegedly drank the rough draft.
Five spirits agreeing to impersonate iced tea. It works exactly once per evening.
The G&T's quieter sibling — tonic doing the talking, vodka holding the coats.
Vodka and cranberry, named for the bogs it drains. The ads wrote themselves.
The Moscow mule gone south — agave in the copper saddle.
Tequila, lime and soda, built tall in the heat. Three things, no argument, no ceremony.
Black rum poured over ginger beer until the cloud forms. Drink it before the weather turns.
Cranberry and pineapple walking vodka down the shore.
The sour formula with dust on its boots. Agave answers the lemon.
Tequila, pineapple, lime, long over ice — the margarita on its holidays.
Bourbon through packed ice and mint, tall enough for the sprig to stand in.
A julep that traded the silver cup for lemon and got quicker about it.
Vodka in a sugar-rimmed lemon suit. Dessert, filing paperwork as a drink.
Gin blushing with grenadine. Prohibition's most respectable alibi.
Rum stacked on rum under fruit. The umbrella is structural.
The missing link between the manhattan and the martini, mixed on gold-rush gin and a twist.
A negroni that swapped gin for bourbon and moved to Paris to write.
The negroni's tequila cousin, printed small and loved late.
Cuba's statesman: rum, vermouth, curaçao and a whisper of grenadine. Wears its coupe like office.
Fleming wrote it for Bond: gin, vodka, and a name he could not keep.
The house pour for the last guest of the night. The book keeps the page; the bar keeps the reason.
